readerTitle: Two new hires, same Monday: why one quit by week three
caseNote: 가상 사례 (가정 청소 업체, 철물 유통 창고, 소프트웨어 회사 고객지원팀) + 실제 연구 프레임워크 (Bauer의 온보딩 4C)
insight: 채용은 계약서 서명에서 끝나지 않는다. 온보딩은 채용의 마지막 단계이며, 좋은 사람을 뽑은 투자가 회수될지 여기서 갈린다.
misconception: 좋은 사람을 뽑으면 알아서 적응한다. 온보딩은 서류 작성과 안전 교육이면 충분하다.

sources.text: Bauer, T. N. (2010). Onboarding New Employees: Maximizing Success. SHRM Foundation Effective Practice Guidelines Series.
청소 업체, 창고, 소프트웨어 회사 사례는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: Bauer(2010) SHRM Foundation 보고서의 '4C'(Compliance, Clarification, Culture, Connection) 구분과 명칭이 원문과 일치하는지 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드에는 수치를 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Two new hires, same Monday. One quit by week three.
body: A home-cleaning company and a hardware warehouse each hired someone on the same Monday. Both hires were solid. Both had passed good interviews.
Six weeks later, one was hitting targets. The other had stopped answering the phone. The difference started on day one.

image.label: Two new workers arriving on the same Monday at different workplaces
image.brief: 화면을 좌우로 나눈 일러스트. 왼쪽은 청소 도구를 든 신입이 낯선 집 현관 앞에 혼자 서 있고, 오른쪽은 창고 입구에서 동료가 신입에게 손을 흔들며 맞이함. 같은 달력 'Monday'가 양쪽 위에 걸려 있음. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your new cleaner starts Monday.
body: You run a home-cleaning company with six crews. You've just hired Sam, who has cleaned hotels before. Your crews are busy and short-handed.
How do you run Sam's first week?

options.text: Put Sam with your fastest crew lead and let Sam learn on the job
options.feedback: Real work and a skilled model help. But your fastest cleaner isn't automatically a good teacher, and nobody has said what "good" looks like in a client's home.

options.text: Give Sam the handbook and safety videos, then a full schedule of jobs
options.feedback: Sam is covered on the rules but alone with the hard parts: picky clients, which products go where, who to call. That's when new hires quietly decide to leave.

options.text: Plan the week: a named buddy, a short checklist per home, one supervised job on day one, a check-in on Friday
options.feedback: It costs a few hours of a buddy's time. In return Sam knows what good looks like and who to ask, and gets feedback before bad habits set in.

cards.title: Same kind of hire. Different first month.
body: The cleaning company did what most busy firms do. Sam got a uniform, a key list and a spot on a crew. Clients complained about missed rooms. Nobody told Sam why. Sam quit in week three.

The warehouse had a one-page plan. Before day one, the new picker's login and boots were ready. A buddy walked the aisles with her. By Friday she had picked real orders and knew her target for week four.

image.label: Side by side: a confused cleaner alone versus a warehouse worker with a buddy
image.brief: 좌우 비교 장면. 왼쪽: 청소부가 고객 집 거실에서 메모 없이 혼자 두리번거리고, 뒤에서 고객이 팔짱을 낀 채 바라봄. 오른쪽: 창고 선반 사이에서 동료가 태블릿을 보여주며 신입과 함께 걸음. 오른쪽 벽에 'Week 1 plan' 종이 한 장. 실제 로고 금지.

cards.title: Onboarding
body: **Onboarding** is the planned path from "signed the offer" to "doing the job well without help." It's the last stage of hiring, not an HR form.
A good hire who never learns how your place works can perform like a bad hire. You spent time and money finding the person. The first month decides whether that spending pays off.

cards.title: Four things every new hire needs.
body: Talya Bauer, a researcher who studies how people join organizations, describes four levels of onboarding in a guide for the SHRM Foundation:
list: **Clarification:** what the job is and what good looks like
**Culture:** how things really get done here
**Connection:** people to ask and work with
cards.callout: Many businesses stop at the first level. Sam got compliance and nothing else.
cards.softwareNote: In a software team, clarification often means a first small task shipped in week one, and connection means a named person to ask, not just a busy group chat.

cards.title: The warehouse's one-page plan.
body: None of this is expensive. It just has to be decided before the person arrives.

breakdown.label: One real task
breakdown.detail: Pick a short order with the buddy

breakdown.label: Clear target
breakdown.detail: What "good" looks like by week four

breakdown.label: Check-in
breakdown.detail: What's hard, what's unclear, what's next

cards.title: Onboarding can't rescue the wrong hire.
body: A good plan speeds up a good fit. It won't turn someone who can't do the job into someone who can. That's what the earlier hiring steps are for.
It also costs time. A buddy who works slower for a week needs that counted, not just piled on top. And more isn't better: dumping every policy on day one buries the few things that matter.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: You run a 20-person software company. A new customer support hire starts Monday, fully remote. Your team is swamped with tickets.
Which first week fits what you've learned?

options.text: Send the login, the help docs and a team-chat welcome; assign tickets from day one
options.feedback: Fast on paper. But remote hires can't overhear how colleagues handle tricky customers, so mistakes stay hidden until a customer complains.

options.text: A week of reading docs and watching recorded calls before touching any tickets
options.feedback: Safe, and the context helps. But a week with no real work delays feedback and can leave the new hire unsure they're needed.

options.text: A buddy on daily video calls, a few easy tickets reviewed on day one, a clear target for week four
options.feedback: It slows the buddy a little at first. It gives the new hire real work, quick feedback and a person to ask, which matters even more when nobody sits nearby.

cards.title: Hiring ends when the new person can do the job, not when they sign.
body: Plan the first month as carefully as the interview: what good looks like, who to ask, one early real task, and a check-in.
**Try it today:** write one page for your next hire: what's ready before day one, their first real task, their buddy, and what "good" looks like at day 30.
